subject: Recap & next steps — pricing, token volumes, batching & concurrency assumptions

Subject: Recap & next steps — pricing, token volumes, batching & concurrency assumptions

Thanks for taking the call today, Jordan — great to meet you and learn more about Acme Retail's roadmap for personalized product recommendations and post-purchase support. Per our conversation, here's a short recap and proposed next steps so we can size costs and a PoC correctly.

What we heard (please correct if I missed anything):
- Initial integration: chat + short-form generation for product Q&A, ~5–10M tokens/month on launch.
- Growth target: 50–100M tokens/month within 6–9 months as recommendation traffic ramps.
- Typical request profile: avg prompt 150 tokens, avg response 400 tokens (total ~550 tokens/request).
- Traffic pattern: steady daytime usage with predictable peaks during marketing campaigns; expect sustained QPS rather than large bursty spikes.
- Budget: initial monthly budget in the $2k–$5k range; willingness to commit to higher spend if unit economics align.

Pricing & unit economics (high-level):
- Baseline list (hosted): ~ $40 / 1M tokens (depends on model family & seq length).
- With continuous batching + KV/prefix caching and a longer-lived steady QPS, we typically see effective cost reductions in the 50–75% range on per-token unit cost for high-volume workloads — realistic delivered range: $12–$20 / 1M tokens depending on sequence length and cache hit rates.
- Target you mentioned: ~ $10–$15 / 1M tokens. We'll test to see if that is achievable given your sequence lengths and hit-rate expectations.

Batching & concurrency assumptions we want to validate:
- Continuous batching assumption: traffic needs to be relatively steady (not purely spiky) so the service can accumulate micro-batches across concurrent requests. For your daytime steady QPS profile, continuous batching should be effective.
- Concurrency: For latency-sensitive product recommendations we aim to keep p95 latency < 300ms. With moderate concurrency (20–100 concurrent requests across your fleet) continuous batching + auto-batching windows of 10–30ms can reduce per-token cost while preserving p95.
- Cache opportunities: product metadata prefix caching (stable prompts) can reduce downstream token generation by up to ~30% in our experience.

Next steps:
1) Can you confirm expected monthly token run-rate for the first quarter (pick low/expected/high)?
2) Can you share a small redacted sample of typical prompts/responses so our SREs can estimate cache hit rates and sequence length distribution? (We included an example spreadsheet attachment for effort estimate.)
3) We'll run a quick internal cost model and propose an initial PoC plan and expected per-1M token unit economics.

Attaching: MA_planning_sheet.xlsx (light planning worksheet) and a short Redwood pricing estimate PDF.

Thanks — I’ll loop in Aditya to follow up on batching/concurrency details and a recommended PoC config.

—Camila

Hi Jordan — quick technical follow-up on batching/concurrency and unit econ expectations. TL;DR: continuous batching can help at surprisingly low sustained QPS if traffic is steady, but realized savings depend on sequence length distribution and cacheability.

Detailed notes:
- Minimum effective QPS: For continuous batching benefits we look for a sustained average QPS > ~2–3 requests/sec across the endpoint. That doesn't mean 2–3 QPS from a single client — it can be aggregated across your traffic (multiple users/clients). For your expected 8M tokens/month and ~550 tokens/request, that's ~14.5k requests/month (~0.0056 req/sec avg) — so at pilot scale continuous batching benefits will be limited unless you concentrate traffic or run synthetic fan-in (e.g., a mid-tier edge pool).
- Burst vs steady: If daytime traffic is steady with modest peaks, continuous batching windows (10–30ms) allow us to merge requests into larger matrix ops and reduce per-token compute. If traffic is very sparse (few requests/sec), latency-preserving timeouts will keep batches small and cost advantages shrink.
- Sequence length: Shorter average sequences reduce amortization benefits per batch. Your avg of ~550 tokens/request still gives room for batching because backend kernels scale with total tokens in a batch. Longer sequences see more benefit due to GPU kernel throughput.
- KV/prefix cache: If you have stable prompt prefixes (e.g., product metadata, templated prompts), caching can cut token generation by ~20–40% in practice; that improves unit economics more than batching alone in low-QPS conditions.

Recommendation for PoC:
1) Pilot config: dedicate a small steady pool with moderate concurrency (10–30) for the west region traffic to accumulate better batching; measure p50/p95 latency and cache hit-rate over 72 hours.
2) Synthetic pressure test: run a 1-hour concentrated run to estimate continuous batching uplift at higher concurrency levels (this helps project costs at scale).
3) Deliverable: an estimated unit-cost table with three scenarios (pilot, steady-state 30M/mo, scale 100M+/mo) and recommended model/quantization profile.

I'll prepare the cost table once we see the prompt sample and a short request histogram. Happy to run a quick benchmark next week if you can provide a small traffic capture (redacted).
